books.section: Topic 7.3 The Spanish-American War and Its Aftermath

primary_sources: President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898

stimulus.source_note: President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898, public domain (abridged).
stimulus.text: "First. In the cause of humanity and to put an end to the barbarities, bloodshed, starvation, and horrible miseries now existing there, and which the parties to the conflict are either unable or unwilling to stop or mitigate. It is no answer to say this is all in another country, belonging to another nation, and is therefore none of our business. It is specially our duty, for it is right at our door. Second. We owe it to our citizens in Cuba to afford them that protection and indemnity for life and property which no government there can or will afford. . . . Third. The right to intervene may be justified by the very serious injury to the commerce, trade, and business of our people, and by the wanton destruction of property and devastation of the island." — President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim abridged excerpt from President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898, public domain
stem: Which later American action would be hardest to square with McKinley's stated reasons in this message?

options.text: The Teller Amendment's promise to leave Cuba
options.misconception: The Teller Amendment fits the message: it promises to leave Cuba to its people once Spain is out.

options.text: The decision to keep the Philippines as a colony
The naval victory at Manila Bay
options.misconception: A battle is not a policy; winning at Manila Bay does not contradict the reasons for intervening in Cuba.

options.text: The Rough Riders' charge at San Juan Hill
options.misconception: The charge was a battle in Cuba, the very intervention the message asks Congress to authorize.

rationales.A: The Teller Amendment echoes the message: free Cuba, then leave it to its people. It fits, it does not clash.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the message is about Cuba, yet the war ended with America keeping the Philippines, a colony thousands of miles away.
rationales.C: Manila Bay was a naval victory in the war McKinley asked for. Victories do not contradict the reasons for fighting.
rationales.D: San Juan Hill was part of the Cuban campaign the message authorized. The fighting matches the request.
rationales.general:
1. Bound the message. Every reason McKinley gives is about Cuba: its suffering, its Americans, its trade.
2. Look at the outcome. The war ended with the United States keeping the Philippines, far from Cuba.
3. Compare the two. A colony in Asia goes beyond anything the message asked Congress to approve.
Remember: to test a stated reason, hold the outcome next to it and ask whether the reason covers what happened.
